structured_output.summary: The hypothesis tree is empty, so this search set the starting point. The most useful find is a public submission to this same benchmark (AIDDA-Institute/CIFAR-100-speedrun) by the "futurebiohackers" team (repo abdullah-athar/iterate-futurebiohackers, PR #3). It reaches 75.29–75.48% in 8.11 s on an A100-SXM4-80GB. The organizers' ResNet9 baseline gets 75.36% in 59.3 s. Their recipe is airbench96-style: a frozen 2x2 patch-whitening stem, widths 128/384/576 with 3 convs per group, SGD-Nesterov with lr 9.0, wd 0.012 and momentum 0.85, BN biases at 64x LR, label smoothing 0.3, batch size 1024, 8.5 epochs, lookahead-EMA, alternating flip with translate 2, fp16 with channels_last, and torch.compile max-autotune warmed up in build. Without re-tuning, airbench96 reaches 79.3–79.8% on CIFAR-100, so the architecture has room above the target. GPU time is about 95% conv, BatchNorm and GELU kernels. That means further gains must come from fewer FLOPs or fewer epochs, not from data loading. Other speedrun work has cut time through progressive resizing (24→28→32 px, −7.6% on CIFAR-10), SiLU, SVD whitening init, brightness/contrast augmentation, CUDA graphs and fused optimizers (hiverge, 2.59→1.98 s), and hard-example selection with a small proxy model (airbench96_faster keeps the top-50%-loss examples). Muon beat SGD on CIFAR-10 airbench94, but the CIFAR-100 team found it lost to SGD at every width. TTA cannot be used here. Precomputing augmentations in build, waiting for the GPU to cool and rerolling for a faster host are explicitly flagged as specification gaming. Of these, only the cooldown is directly named in the task rules ("no sleeps"); the other two are rejected as gaming in the source write-up. Seed-to-seed std is about 0.25 pp on CIFAR-100, so a 3-seed mean has an SE of about 0.15 pp. That makes the 0.753 gate tight for recipes that score around 75.3–75.5% over 40 seeds.

findings.claim: A public submission to this same CIFAR-100 benchmark reached a mean of 75.29% (PR text; the repo README says 75.48%, sd 0.25 pp) in 8.11 s (sd 0.02) over 40 trials on an A100-SXM4-80GB. Exact defaults: epochs 8.5, bs 1024, lr 9.0 (divided by kilostep_scale = 1024*(1+1/(1-mom))), momentum 0.85 with Nesterov, wd 0.012*bs/kilostep_scale, bias_scaler 64, label_smoothing 0.3, warmup 0.23 (from 0.2 to 1.0) then linear decay to 0.07, whiten_bias_epochs 3, translate 2 (reflect pad), alternating flip, no cutout, widths [128,384,576], depth 3 (3 convs per group with a residual over the last two), MaxPool2d(2) per group then MaxPool2d(3), BN with frozen weight, eps 1e-12 and bn_momentum 0.6, GELU, logits*1/9, 2x2 whitening conv with 24 channels initialized from 5000 training images in prepare, lookahead-EMA every 5 steps with decay 0.95^5*(step/total)^3, fp16 + channels_last, torch.compile max-autotune. Build warms up on 50k random uint8 images by running prepare plus a partial fit twice and evaluating several batch sizes.
findings.relevance: This gives a ready-made feasible starting point that is about 7x faster than the organizers' baseline (59.3 s). The first experiment should reproduce it rather than tune the ResNet9 baseline.
hypotheses: New H1: an airbench96-style net (whitening stem, 3-conv groups, SGD lr 9, bias 64x, LS 0.3, lookahead-EMA) hits ≥75.3% in about 8–9 s on this machine
New H1.1: reproducing the futurebiohackers defaults gives accuracy ≥0.753 on seeds 0–2 with time ≤9 s

findings.claim: Ablations on CIFAR-100: the airbench94 net at 12 ep got 70.6% in 3.5 s. The airbench96 net (128/384/512, 3 convs) at 12 ep got 76.0% in 9.4 s. 9 ep with last block 576 got 75.6% in 8.58 s. 8 ep with last block 768 got 75.6% in 8.40 s. 8.5 ep with last block 576 got 75.5% in 8.11 s. 3-conv groups beat widening 2-conv groups. Widening the last block (7x7/3x3 spatial) adds accuracy cheaply. Muon 'lost to SGD at every size'. Label smoothing 0.3 beat 0.2 and 0.4. About 95% of GPU time is in conv, BN and GELU kernels.
findings.relevance: This maps the trade-off between epochs, width and accuracy near the threshold. The last block is the cheap place to add capacity, and the remaining cost is in compute kernels, not data loading.
hypotheses: H: moving capacity into group 3 (wider, e.g. 768–1024) while cutting epochs below 8 reduces time at constant accuracy
H: switching GELU to a cheaper activation (ReLU/SiLU) or fusing BN+activation reduces time per epoch without hurting accuracy
H: Muon on CIFAR-100 is not a win (prior evidence against it)

findings.claim: Epochs saved on CIFAR-10 to reach 94%: patch-whitening init about 13 epochs (more than doubles speed), dirac/identity init about 1.2, BN-bias LR x64 about 1.7, lookahead about 1.5, alternating flip about 1.1, multi-crop TTA about 0.7. Effects are roughly additive. airbench96 without re-tuning reaches 79.27% on CIFAR-100 (79.76% with cutout) vs ResNet-18 at 77.5–78.0%. Seed std on CIFAR-10 is about 0.12–0.16%.
findings.relevance: This shows which components matter most. The futurebiohackers recipe may not use dirac init (not listed in its extracted code), which could save an estimated 1 epoch. TTA is banned here, so its contribution is lost.
hypotheses: New H: adding dirac/identity init to the 3-conv groups lets epochs drop by 0.5–1 at the same accuracy

findings.claim: The CIFAR-10 94% record went from 2.59 s to 1.98 s with: a vectorized/batched Muon (padded matrices, batched Newton-Schulz), vectorized batch cropping, a compiled forward/backward step, GELU→SiLU, SVD whitening init, brightness/contrast augmentation, fp16 + channels_last, hyperparameter retuning and selective TTA. No per-change breakdown was published.
findings.relevance: These are systems and architecture tweaks that may carry over: compiling the whole training step, vectorized augmentation, SiLU, SVD whitening. Selective TTA is not allowed here.
hypotheses: New H: compiling the full train step (forward+backward+optimizer) or capturing it with CUDA graphs cuts per-step overhead measurably at bs 1024
New H: brightness/contrast augmentation lets epochs drop at equal accuracy on CIFAR-100

findings.claim: Progressive resizing (24×24 → 28×28 after a few epochs → 32×32 for the rest) saved 0.150 s off 1.98 s on CIFAR-10 (the main legitimate gain). Pooling optimizations saved 0.062 s and CUDA graphs plus optimizer fusion 0.040 s, for a 7.6% total. The schedule needed slightly more epochs, but early steps were much cheaper. The same write-up flags as specification gaming: precomputing all augmented epochs in untimed setup, a 60 s GPU cooldown sleep, and rerolling for a faster host.
findings.relevance: Progressive resizing is a direct FLOP reduction and could save about 5–10% here. The gaming patterns must be avoided: this task's rules ban sleeps and require real-data work in prepare/train. Compile must be warmed up for each resolution in build to avoid recompiles during timed training.
hypotheses: New H: progressive resizing (e.g. 24→28→32 px) cuts time by ≥5% with accuracy ≥0.753 if each shape is warmed up in build

findings.claim: airbench96_faster (96% on CIFAR-10 in 27.3 s vs 34.7 s for legacy airbench96) uses a small proxy net (widths 32/64/64, depth 2) to score losses on each 1024-example batch and trains the main net only on the 512 highest-loss examples. Selective-Backprop reports up to 3.5x faster convergence to target error on CIFAR-10/100 by backpropagating only high-loss examples.
findings.relevance: Hard-example selection is a known way to reduce wall-clock at longer schedules. At about 8 epochs it is uncertain whether the proxy cost pays off, and with 100 classes and 500 images per class, dropping data may hurt more than on CIFAR-10.
hypotheses: New H: loss-based example selection (keeping the top ~50–70% by loss after epoch 1–2) reduces time at ≥0.753 on CIFAR-100

findings.claim: airbench94_muon: bs 2000, 8 epochs, Muon (lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, 3 Newton-Schulz steps) on conv filters. SGD for biases/head (lr 0.053/0.67, momentum 0.85). Label smoothing 0.2, BN momentum 0.6 with frozen weight, GELU, widths 64/256/256, compile max-autotune. 94.01% in 2.59 s vs 3.09 s for compiled SGD airbench94.
findings.relevance: Muon helped on CIFAR-10, but the only CIFAR-100 evidence (futurebiohackers) says it lost to SGD. It is worth at most one cheap check, with a larger batch size (2000) as a separate variable.
hypotheses: H: batch size 2000 (fewer, larger steps) reduces time at equal epochs without dropping accuracy

findings.claim: Official judging is on an A100 80GB PCIe (300 W) over 40 trials. The score is mean prepare+train time. Prepare (GPU transfer, preprocessing) is deliberately timed. The organizers' baseline is a ResNet9 (width 64, 40 epochs) at 75.36% in 59.30 s. The repo shows no public PRs/leaderboard entries yet.
findings.relevance: Confirms that work like whitening init and normalization must stay in the timed prepare, and that the PCIe judge will be somewhat slower than the SXM dev GPU.
hypotheses: H: work in prepare (uint8→fp16 normalization on GPU, whitening eigendecomposition on 5000 images) is a small but non-zero share of time that can be optimized (e.g. fewer images for whitening, fused normalization)
